Introduction

1.1 This Guide is a practical guide. It should not be relied on as a statement of the law. Parties who wish to understand their rights and obligations fully should study the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, as amended by the Employment Rights Act 2025, the Trade Unions (Right to Access Workplaces) Regulations 2026, the Trade Unions (Right to Access Workplaces) (Required Information) Regulations 2026 and the Code of Practice: Right of trade unions to access workplaces, or seek legal advice. Further non-statutory guidance may be published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade.

1.2 This Guide is intended to assist parties dealing with the CAC under the statutory right of access framework. It does not repeat the Code of Practice. The Code gives detailed guidance on the conduct expected of unions and employers when access requests are made, considered and negotiated, and on the principles and factors relevant to workplace access. Parties should consult the Code alongside this Guide, and any CAC forms or notes issued for right of access applications or complaints.

1.3 Throughout this Guide, references to “union” should be read as references to “unions” in cases where an application is brought by more than one union. References to “employer” should include any person treated as an employer for the purposes of the relevant provisions. References to “workplace” should be read as references to “workplaces” where appropriate. References to “the parties” mean the union and the employer involved in the access request, access agreement or related CAC proceedings. References to a “working day” is any day that is not: a Saturday or Sunday; Christmas Day; Good Friday; or a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971 in the relevant part of Great Britain.

The Central Arbitration Committee

2.1 The Central Arbitration Committee (CAC) is an independent tribunal with statutory powers. Its Chair is Stephen Redmond. The CAC has responsibilities in areas including trade union recognition and derecognition, the disclosure of information for collective bargaining, applications and complaints related to information and consultation arrangements, statutory workplace access matters, and disputes over the establishment of European Works Councils where negotiations commenced, but were not concluded before 1 January 2021, and disputes over the operation of European Works Councils.

2.2 The CAC’s aim is to achieve fair and lasting solutions to disputes, having regard to the continuing relationship between the parties. Its approach is flexible and one of problem-solving. Where appropriate, the CAC will encourage the parties to agree effective workplace arrangements.

2.3 The CAC is composed of the Chair, Deputy Chairs and members with experience as representatives of employers and employees. Members are drawn from a wide range of industries and services in the public and private sectors and have extensive experience in industrial relations. A Panel will be appointed to deal with each right of access application or complaint received by the CAC. A CAC Case Manager will also be appointed. The Case Manager will act as the main point of contact for the parties and will explain the CAC’s procedures. Although the CAC is required to make decisions under the statutory provisions, it will, where appropriate, encourage the parties to resolve matters by agreement. The provisions allow for an application to be considered by a Panel Chair sitting alone. Paragraph 9.6 below explains the circumstances in which this may happen.

The right of access provisions

3.1 The right of access provisions enables a qualifying independent trade union to request access to a workplace for statutory access purposes. These purposes are meeting, supporting, representing, recruiting or organising workers, and facilitating collective bargaining, but do not include organising industrial action. Access is subject to the limits set out in the legislation and the Code of Practice.

3.2 Access may involve physical entry to a workplace, communication with workers by digital or other means, or both. Access arrangements should not unreasonably interfere with the employer’s business and may include appropriate conditions or safeguards where necessary.

Making an access request

4.1 Before making an application to the CAC, the union must have made a written and dated access request to the employer. Unions should use the Union Request Template, which can be found on the CAC’s website. The request must contain specific information required by the legislation and must have been given to the employer in the manner required by the legislation. Further guidance on making an application to the CAC is set out at paragraph 5.1.

4.2 The employer’s response period ends at the end of the 15th working day after the day on which the access request is given. If the employer gives a response notice before the end of that period and the terms of access are not agreed, the parties then enter into the negotiation period. The negotiation period ends at the end of the 25th working day after the day on which the response notice is given.

4.3 Where the parties enter into an access agreement by negotiation, they must jointly notify the CAC of the terms of that agreement by e-mail: Access@cac.gov.uk. The notification may be given by either party on behalf of both parties. It must be in writing and dated, confirm that the agreement is being entered into under the statutory right of access framework, be signed by or on behalf of both parties, and include a copy of the access agreement. A proforma for this purpose can be found on the CAC’s website at www.cac.gov.uk.

11.3 The procedure at the hearing is orderly but seeks to avoid unnecessary formality. Each party will be asked to comment on and amplify its written statement, to comment on the other party’s evidence and to answer questions put by the Panel. The Panel Chair may allow questions to be put to speakers or witnesses where this is necessary to deal with factual issues.

11.4 Hearings will normally be arranged as quickly as possible and will normally be completed in a day.

CAC determinations, declarations and orders

12.1 Where the CAC determines that access should take place, its determination will specify the form of access, the workers or categories of workers covered, the workplace or workplaces concerned, timing, frequency, duration, location, digital channels and any reasonable conditions or safeguards. Where the CAC deals with a complaint alleging breach of an access agreement, it may declare whether the complaint is well-founded and, where appropriate, make an order requiring specified steps to be taken. Complaints and breaches are explained further at paragraphs 8.1 to 8.7.

12.2 CAC determinations, declarations and orders are published on the CAC’s website.

Appeals

13.1 A party may appeal to the Employment Appeal Tribunal against a CAC determination or order made under the statutory right of access provisions. This includes an appeal against a penalty order made by the CAC under the enforcement provisions.

User Satisfaction

If you are asked for your views on any aspect of our service, we would appreciate your cooperation. But if you have comments, whether of satisfaction, complaint or suggestion, please do not wait to be asked. If you are dissatisfied with any aspect of our service, please let us know so that we can put things right. If you cannot resolve the problem with the person who dealt with you originally, please ask to speak to the Operations Manager or, if necessary, the Chief Executive who will investigate your complaint. If you wish to complain in writing, please send an email to enquiries@cac.gov.uk for the attention of Maverlie Tavares, Chief Executive or post it to the above address.

In the event of any complaint, we hope that you will let us try to put things right. But, if necessary, you can write to your MP who can tell you how to have your complaint referred to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration (the Ombudsman).
